passage:
Dear Gargi Masi,
At Sunday lunch I told everyone about the night the roof leaked at Nani's house and we all slept in the kitchen by a lantern. I can see it: the drip into the steel bucket, your blue shawl over my feet, the smell of kerosene.
Then Mummy and you both said it never happened. Nani's house has a concrete roof, and I only stayed there in summer. I was hurt, honestly. It felt as if you were taking away something that was mine.
I've been thinking since. Maybe I built it from your stories about your own childhood there. It still feels so real that letting go of it is strange.
Could you tell me the lantern story again, properly? I want to know whose memory it is.
Love, Harsha

qa.q: What did Mummy and Gargi Masi say about the leaking roof?
qa.a: They said it never happened, since Nani's house has a concrete roof and Harsha only stayed there in summer.

qa.q: Why did Harsha feel hurt when told the leak never happened?
qa.a: The memory was so vivid, with the drip, the blue shawl and the kerosene smell, that losing it felt like having something taken away.

qa.q: What step does Harsha take towards understanding the memory?
qa.a: Harsha asks Gargi Masi to tell the lantern story again, properly, to find out whose memory it really is.

qa.q: How might Gargi Masi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: She might be touched that her childhood stories stayed so strongly with Harsha, and a little sorry the correction at lunch hurt. 🤍

grounding: It shows a young adult with a vivid, emotional childhood memory that family members say never happened.

Rekha, is the mic on? Okay. My strangest memory: I was sure I got lost at the zoo when I was four. I can see the tall bars, a zookeeper in a green cap, and an announcement with my name, Simran, echoing everywhere.
I told that story at every sleepover. Last year at a family wedding I told it again, and my dad said, "Simran, we never took you to the zoo at four. You got lost in a shop for two minutes." My brother nodded. Two minutes!
I actually argued with them. The green cap felt more real than my own birthday.
It shook me. If something that vivid can come from my own head, what else can? I still love the story. I just call it "my zoo story" now, not "the day I got lost".

qa.q: Where did Simran's dad say Simran really got lost?
qa.a: In a shop, for two minutes.

qa.q: Why did Simran argue with the family at first?
qa.a: The green cap and the echoing announcement felt more real than Simran's own birthday, so the memory seemed impossible to doubt.

qa.q: How does Simran choose to hold the memory now?
qa.a: Simran still enjoys it but calls it "my zoo story" instead of "the day I got lost", treating it as a story rather than proof.

qa.q: How might Simran's dad have felt correcting the story at the wedding?
qa.a: He may have felt amused or a bit awkward correcting a favourite story in front of relatives, while wanting the facts straight.

I'm Kiran, Salma's roommate, so I heard this one live. Salma was video-calling her family and said, "Remember when Abbu carried me on his shoulders through the flood water? I was holding the umbrella." She described it all: the brown water, the red umbrella, the shop shutters.
Her mother went quiet. Then her brother said, "Salma, there was never a flood. You saw that in a film at Khala's house."
Salma laughed at first, then didn't. After the call she sat on her bed for a long time with her knees pulled up. She said, "I can still feel the umbrella handle."
I don't know what was going on in her head. I just made tea and didn't take either side.

qa.q: What colour was the umbrella in Salma's memory?
qa.a: The umbrella was red.

qa.q: What might Salma be feeling as she sits with her knees pulled up?
qa.a: She seems unsettled and confused, because the memory feels real enough to touch, yet her family says it never happened.

qa.q: What could help Salma make sense of the memory?
qa.a: She could ask her family calmly about the film at Khala's house, and treat the memory as meaningful without needing every detail to be true.

qa.q: How does Kiran respond, and why might that help Salma?
qa.a: Kiran makes tea and takes neither side, which gives Salma space to feel unsettled without being pushed.

It walked right into this courtyard, spread its tail, and I fed it a bit of my roti. I can still hear it screaming." Nani laughed. "No peacock ever came here, beti. Never." Irawati's mother shook her head too.
Monday: Back at college, Irawati couldn't let it go. She told her friend Asif, "I can see the blue of its neck. How can that not be real?" Asif shrugged. "Maybe you saw one somewhere else?"
Thursday: Her mother phoned. She had found an old album: Irawati, four, at a zoo in Delhi, holding roti out to a peacock behind a fence. Irawati looked at the photo for a long time. The feeling was real. The courtyard wasn't.

passage: Simran, beti, you told that well story again at dinner, eyes shining: you, six years old, falling into the farm well, the cold water, your Dadu pulling you out by your plait. You told it so well your cousins went quiet. Now let your Rekha Dadi tell you what I remember, since I was there. There was no fall. It was your cousin Gunjan who slipped into the irrigation channel, knee-deep, and your Dadu lifted her out, laughing. You were on the charpai with me, eating a guava, and you cried because everyone ran to Gunjan. For years afterwards you begged to hear that story. Somewhere along the way it became yours. I'm not saying you're lying, beti. Your heart remembers the fright. But a memory can be bright and strong and still not have happened.

qa.q: Who actually slipped into the irrigation channel?
qa.a: Her cousin Gunjan, knee-deep.

qa.q: Why does Simran's well story feel so real to her?
qa.a: She heard the family story so often and felt the fright of that day so strongly that the vivid version became her own memory.

qa.q: How could Simran hold this memory differently from now on?
qa.a: She could treat the feeling as real but the details as uncertain, and check with family before telling it as fact.

qa.q: What might it be like for Gunjan to hear Simran tell the story as her own?
qa.a: Gunjan might be puzzled or a little put out, hearing her own scary moment told as someone else's.

grounding: A grandmother tells a young woman that her vivid, emotional childhood memory of falling into a well never happened to her.

Note after Sunday lunch. Jagdish.
Rashmi is twenty now, home from college, and at lunch she told a story I had never heard: the day she was five and got lost at the Dussehra fair, and a policeman carried her on his shoulders to the loudspeaker stall. She described his moustache, the red lights, the smell of jalebis. She was close to tears telling it. Her mother and I looked at each other. It never happened. We never took her to that fair; she had chickenpox that year. But I didn't laugh. I told her gently that we had no memory of it, and asked where she thought it came from. She went quiet, then said her cousin used to tell a story just like that about himself. We sat together for a while. It clearly felt real to her, and that part matters.

qa.q: Why could Rashmi not have been at the fair that year?
qa.a: She had chickenpox that year.

qa.q: Why was Rashmi close to tears telling the story?
qa.a: Rashmi felt moved and frightened recalling it, because the scene was vivid and emotional, even though it never happened to her.

qa.q: How did Jagdish respond, and why was it kind?
qa.a: Jagdish didn't laugh, gently told Rashmi that the family had no memory of it, and asked where it might have come from, respecting that it felt real.

qa.q: How did Rashmi's mother react at lunch?
qa.a: Her mother exchanged a look with Jagdish, knowing it never happened, and joined in handling it gently.

passage:
Thursday night
Had the strangest conversation with Chinmay today. I was telling my roommate about the time I fell out of Ajoba's mango tree when I was eight and broke my arm. I remember everything: the rough bark, the snap, the smell of the hospital, the pink cast everyone signed. Chinmay, visiting, laughed. "Deepu, that was me. I broke my arm. You were the one who ran for help." I told him no way. He sent me a photo from Aai's album: Chinmay, eight, with a white cast, and me beside him, holding his hand.
I've been staring at the photo all night. The pink cast I remember doesn't exist. The feeling of falling feels completely real. How can a memory this vivid be wrong?
Deepika

qa.q: What colour was the cast in the photo?
qa.a: White.

qa.q: How does Deepika feel staring at the photo all night?
qa.a: Deepika feels shaken and confused, because the memory of falling feels completely real even though the photo shows it happened to Chinmay.

qa.q: What could Deepika take from this about vivid memories?
qa.a: That vividness and emotion don't prove a memory is accurate, so checking photos or asking family is wise before being certain.

qa.q: How did Chinmay react to Deepika's version?
qa.a: Chinmay laughed, then sent the photo to show it was his arm that broke and that Deepika ran for help.

grounding: Shows a young adult with a vivid memory of a fall that a brother and a photo show happened to him.

Samir, twenty, was home in Bareilly for the holidays. At dinner, he told the story he'd told a hundred times: when he was four, his uncle Rafiq carried him on his shoulders through the fair, and he got a pink balloon shaped like a fish.

"Samir," his mother said gently, "Rafiq chacha was in Dubai that whole year."

"No, he carried me. I remember the fish."

Rafiq, visiting now, laughed. "I never went to that fair. I think your Nana took you."

Samir went quiet. The memory felt warm, bright and absolutely real. He could smell the fried jalebi. But it seemed it hadn't happened the way he remembered.

"Maybe the balloon's real," he said slowly. "Just not the shoulders."

qa.q: Where was Rafiq chacha that whole year?
qa.a: In Dubai.

qa.q: How did Samir feel when his mother and Rafiq said it didn't happen?
qa.a: He felt confused and a little sad, because the memory felt warm and absolutely real.

qa.q: What would you advise Samir about this memory?
qa.a: Keep enjoying the memory but accept that parts of it, like the shoulders, may be mixed up, as he starts to do at the end.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel hearing his nephew's story?
qa.a: Rafiq seems amused and warm, maybe touched that Samir remembered him so fondly.

Omar, twenty-one, was studying in Toronto and video-calling his sister Fatima in Cairo. He brought up a story he loved: when he was six, they'd found a stray kitten on the roof and hidden it in the laundry basket for a week.

Fatima laughed. "Omar, that never happened."

"Of course it did. It was grey with a white paw. I named it Cloud."

"We never had a kitten. You wanted one. You drew pictures of a grey kitten named Cloud."

Omar sat back. The memory was so vivid, the soft fur, the basket, the fear of getting caught.

"Are you sure?"

"I'm sure. But I can see why it feels real," Fatima said softly.

qa.q: What did Omar say the kitten was named?
qa.a: Cloud.

qa.q: How did Omar feel when Fatima said it never happened?
qa.a: He felt shocked and unsettled, because he could remember the soft fur and his fear of getting caught.

qa.q: What could Omar take from this about his other childhood memories?
qa.a: He could enjoy them but remember that vivid feelings don't prove every detail happened.

qa.q: How does Fatima respond to Omar's confusion?
qa.a: Fatima is gentle and understanding, saying she can see why it feels real.

passage:
At the college counselling centre's group session on memory, the leader asked students to share a childhood memory they were sure of.

Ankita, nineteen, told hers: at five, she'd been chased by a buffalo on her grandmother's farm and hid in the hay. She described the smell, the noise, the fear.

After the session, her friend Uday, who grew up in the same village, looked puzzled. "Your Nani didn't have buffaloes. Only goats."

Ankita frowned. "I'm sure."

That evening she asked her mother on the phone. "That was a story Nani told you, about her own childhood."

Ankita sat on her bed, heart racing. The fear felt so real. How could it not be hers?

qa.q: What animals did Ankita's Nani have, according to Uday?
qa.a: Only goats.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel on her bed after the call?
qa.a: She felt shaken and confused, her heart racing, because the fear felt real even though the event wasn't hers.

qa.q: What could Ankita do with this discovery?
qa.a: She could bring it to the next group session and talk about how stories can become memories, without feeling foolish.

qa.q: How might Uday feel after pointing out the goats?
qa.a: Uday might feel a bit awkward, worried about upsetting a friend.

grounding: A young adult vividly recalls a childhood scene that turns out to be her grandmother's story, as vividness doesn't prove accuracy.

Hi Zeenat,
You asked why I went so quiet at dinner with my family last week. Here's the truth. All my life I've had this memory: standing on our terrace in the rain, Dadi holding a red umbrella over me, a kite stuck on the water tank, Dadi humming an old song. I can smell the wet cement. I brought it up at dinner, all warm, and my parents looked at each other. Mummy said, "Rukmini, we moved to that flat when you were eight, and Dadi never climbed stairs by then." My brother agreed. I felt a kind of grief, like losing a real day. It's still so clear. How can something this vivid be made up? Maybe a photo, or a story someone told. I'm not angry, just shaken.
Rukmini
